idiom_name: Bunny :headers hash plus Rack-style middleware; broker-tracked x-death
implementation_notes: Bunny publishes with a :headers hash (exchange.publish(payload, headers: {'history' => JSON.generate(hops)})) and consumers read the hash from delivery_info, so the classic structure becomes a Rack-style middleware (or a consumer wrapper) that merges one appended hop into the incoming hash. RabbitMQ itself appends dead-letter hops to x-death, so a complete reader takes both sources: your application-level 'history' plus the broker-level array of {queue, reason, count, time} entries. Keep header values AMQP-friendly strings/numbers and bound the list.
code_sketch:
def publish_with_hop(exchange, payload, headers)
  hops = JSON.parse(headers['history']) rescue []
  hops << { 'name' => 'billing', 'ts' => Time.now.utc.iso8601 }
  exchange.publish(payload, headers: headers.merge('history' => JSON.generate(hops)))
end

# consumer side, broker-tracked dead-letter hops:
# info.headers['x-death'] # => [{ 'queue' => ..., 'reason' => 'expired', 'count' => 2 }]
pitfalls: x-death is not a full history: it compresses repeated dead-letterings by {queue, reason} and records only dead-letter events, so it complements rather than replaces an application-level trail.
Header values must survive AMQP encoding: symbols, arbitrary objects and nil values break publication or arrive as bytes, so serialize the hop list to a string.
Parsing partner-supplied headers with JSON.parse (rescued or not) needs bounds and shape validation - an oversized or malformed history is a cheap way to break a consumer.
